name: Gerovital

card.summary: A Romanian procaine preparation (GH3) promoted since the 1950s to counter aging and keep people looking and feeling younger.
card.note: The FDA has barred its importation since 1982 as an unapproved drug.

quick.overview:
Gerovital H3 is a 2% procaine solution developed by Romanian physician Ana Aslan in the 1950s and promoted as an anti-aging treatment. In looks terms, it was marketed to keep elderly people vigorous and youthful.

It drew celebrity clients in the 1960s and 1970s. Trials in the 1970s examined its effects, and later reviews reported weak monoamine oxidase inhibition as a possible antidepressant mechanism.
quick.how: Aslan's clinic offered it as courses of injections; oral and cream versions followed. This is described historically only.
quick.risks: The FDA says it is an unapproved new drug and has barred importation since 1982; a 1994 FDA article reported low blood pressure, breathing difficulty and convulsions in some users [1].

lead: Gerovital H3 (GH3) is a procaine hydrochloride preparation developed in Romania by Ana Aslan (1897-1988), who headed the National Institute of Geriatrics in Bucharest [1]. Promoters presented it as a general anti-aging therapy, aimed at preserving vitality and youthfulness.
In the 1960s and 1970s the Parhon Institute clinic became a destination, with a reported jet-set clientele including Nikita Khrushchev and Konrad Adenauer [1].

In 1973 three British Medical Journal reports found no merit in procaine for aging problems, and later trials suggested weak MAO inhibition with otherwise negligible effects [1]. The FDA has barred importation since 1982 [1].

chain: Procaine injections promoted as slowing aging
Users hope for more vigour and youthful presentation
angle.text: It was marketed to keep older people youthful in health and appearance. Evidence cited is from 1970s geriatric trials rather than cosmetic outcomes.

paras: Ana Aslan promoted Gerovital from the 1950s until her death in 1988 [1]. The Romanian clinic attracted international visitors during the Cold War [1].

The FDA treats Gerovital, GH3 and similar procaine products as unapproved new drugs, banning interstate commerce and importation since 1982; an order was lifted for cosmetic lines without procaine [1]. A 1994 FDA Consumer article stated no health claims were substantiated [1].

In 1973 three simultaneous British Medical Journal reports found no merit in procaine for aging problems; mid-to-late 1970s trials suggested weak monoamine oxidase inhibition, possibly a mild antidepressant effect [1]. A 1990 controlled trial found no effect on rehabilitation in back or hip disease [2].

timeline.event: Three BMJ reports find no merit in procaine for aging [1]
